primitives.name: Binary Encoded Predictors
primitives.verbatim_quote: (c) **BEP (new)**: encode class y as d=⌈log2n⌉-bit code B(y)∈{±1}^d; ψ^BEP(y,u) = (max_j (-B_j(y)·u_j) + 1)_+; pred = abstain if min_j |u_j| ≤ τ else B^{-1}(sign(u)).
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'y': 'class label in {1,...,n}', 'u': 'score vector in ℝ^n', 'B(y)': 'binary code in {±1}^d where d = ⌈log₂n⌉', 'τ': 'threshold in [0,1]'}
primitives.assumptions: Classes are encoded using binary codes; predictor outputs are score vectors; abstention occurs when minimum absolute score falls below threshold.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When min_j |u_j| ≤ τ, prediction is abstained; otherwise, class is inferred via inverse binary decoding.

layer2.mapping: BEP maps n-class prediction to binary vector space, reducing dimensionality from n to log₂(n) while preserving consistency under convex surrogates.
layer2.telemetry: Prediction accuracy and abstention rate at varying τ values.

primitives.name: Crammer-Singer Surrogate
primitives.verbatim_quote: - Three consistent surrogates for abstain-1/2 (with non-standard predictors, not argmax): (a) Crammer-Singer: ψ^CS(y,u) = (max_{j≠y} u_j - u_y + 1)_+, pred = argmax_i u_i if u_(1) - u_(2) > τ_CS else abstain.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'y': 'class label in {1,...,n}', 'u': 'score vector in ℝ^n', 'τ_CS': 'threshold in [0,1]'}
primitives.assumptions: Surrogate loss is defined over pairwise differences; prediction is made based on margin between top two scores.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Abstains when difference between top two scores is insufficient (u_(1) - u_(2) ≤ τ_CS).

layer2.mapping: CS surrogate uses margin-based scoring to define consistent multiclass loss with reject option, suitable for kernel methods.
layer2.telemetry: Margin distribution and abstention frequency under varying τ_CS.

primitives.name: One-vs-All Hinge
primitives.verbatim_quote: (b) One-vs-all hinge: ψ^OVA(y,u) = Σ_i [1(y=i)(1-u_i)_+ + 1(y≠i)(1+u_i)_+], pred = argmax_i u_i if max_j u_j > τ_OVA else abstain.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'y': 'class label in {1,...,n}', 'u': 'score vector in ℝ^n', 'τ_OVA': 'threshold in [0,1]'}
primitives.assumptions: Each class is treated independently through binary classification; hinge loss applied per class.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Abstains when maximum score does not exceed τ_OVA.

layer2.mapping: OVA hinge generalizes binary hinge to multiclass setting, enabling rejection via global score thresholding.
layer2.telemetry: Per-class hinge loss and overall abstention behavior under τ_OVA.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight of [1148] lies in the reduction of multiclass classification with a reject option to convex surrogate optimization over a reduced-dimensional space. The BEP (Binary Encoded Predictors) method encodes each class into a binary vector of length ⌈log₂n⌉, allowing the use of a single scalar-valued function per class instead of n functions. This leads to a significant computational advantage—training time scales logarithmically with n rather than linearly. The key mathematical structure is that the loss function ψ^BEP(y, u) = (max_j (-B_j(y) · u_j) + 1)_+ ensures consistency by penalizing misclassification in terms of dot products between binary codes and score vectors. The dual formulation enables efficient optimization using block coordinate ascent with l1-ball projections. In contrast, Crammer-Singer and One-vs-All hinge approaches rely on pairwise comparisons or individual class scoring respectively, which require more complex computations but still maintain consistency under appropriate conditions. The theoretical guarantee hinges on the fact that the VC dimension of the abstain loss is bounded by ⌈log₂n⌉, significantly smaller than the standard n−1 bound for non-reject settings. This implies that even with a reject option, the number of effective parameters required for consistency grows logarithmically with the number of classes. The failure mode arises when τ is too aggressive (close to 0 or 1), leading to either no abstentions or excessive abstentions, resulting in poor empirical performance. Additionally, the choice of α (abstention cost) must align with the underlying edge distribution for optimal economic outcomes.
